X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Bioelectrical Impedance Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) precision health prediction messaging emphasizing body-fat accuracy and medical evidence; (B) convenience/privacy messaging emphasizing discreet home use and data privacy. Both conditions receive the same price point (e.g., €150) and a brief product description. Participants indicate whether they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 adults aged 25-55 in Japan, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and higher maximum price than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and higher maximum price than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If Condition A’s purchase intent ≥ 35% and maximum price ≥ €170, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on precise health prediction. If Condition B’s purchase intent ≥ 35% and maximum price ≥ €170, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and privacy. If neither condition meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or preference for precise health prediction versus convenience. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether consumers value precise health prediction over convenience/privacy. If the survey meets the decision thresholds, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers in Japan who are willing to pay a premium for precise body-fat analysis and are willing to purchase a home device.
final.value_proposition: A stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyzer marketed as a premium, home health monitoring tool that provides accurate body-fat data and personalized health insights, sold at a price point reflecting medical-grade accuracy.
final.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget, targeting 300 Japanese adults aged 25–55.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence from 1993 on consumer demand for home use, willingness to pay, or preference for precise health prediction versus convenience.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent ≥ 35% and maximum price ≥ €170 for the precision health prediction messaging, indicating T1 is likely.
If the survey shows purchase intent ≥ 35% and maximum price ≥ €170 for the convenience/privacy messaging, indicating T2 is likely.
If the survey fails to meet either threshold, indicating insufficient consumer interest to justify investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capturing margin through sales and potential subscription services for data tracking.
assumptions: Consumers trust medical evidence linking body fat to health outcomes.
Consumers are willing to invest in home health monitoring devices.
Price sensitivity is manageable for the target segment.
predictions: If offered at a price point below €200, purchase intent among health-conscious consumers will be above 15% in a survey.
Repeat purchase rate for subscription services will be higher among those who use the device regularly.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Employers and insurers seek to reduce healthcare costs and improve employee health; they value data-driven interventions and are willing to subsidize devices that lower long-term risks.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell devices at volume discounts and offer subscription services for data analytics, earning recurring revenue from both the employer and the employee.
assumptions: Employers and insurers are willing to invest in preventive health technologies.
Reimbursement for home health monitoring exists or can be secured.
Employees will use the device if it is provided by their employer.
predictions: If offered at a bulk price of €150 per unit, corporate buyers will place orders for at least 500 units within 12 weeks.
Employee participation rate will exceed 30% when the device is provided by the employer.

X1.name: Consumer vs Employer Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Health‑conscious consumers (n=200) and (B) Employer wellness program coordinators (n=200). Each participant views a product description of a home body‑fat analyzer priced at €180 (just below the €200 threshold). They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (binary yes/no). Additionally, for the employer group, they are asked: "Would you recommend your employer purchase this device for a wellness program?" (binary yes/no).
X1.sample: 400 adults: 200 health‑conscious consumers recruited via health‑focused online panels; 200 employer wellness coordinators recruited via HR/benefits firm panels.
X1.measure: Purchase intent for consumers (percentage saying yes) and employer recommendation intent (percentage saying yes).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% (health‑conscious consumers will show interest). Employer recommendation intent ≤ 10% (not enough to drive bulk orders).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Employer recommendation intent ≥ 30% (employers will show interest). Consumer purchase intent ≤ 15% (not enough to justify consumer launch).

X1.decision_rule: If consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% AND employer recommendation intent ≤ 10%, proceed with differentiated consumer proposition targeting health‑conscious consumers. If either condition fails, abandon consumer expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or employer adoption, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Employer Purchase Intent Test (survey 400 participants, €18,000, 10 weeks) to validate demand and willingness to pay before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers seeking weight management and fitness tracking, and corporate wellness programs willing to subsidize devices.
final.value_proposition: A home body‑fat analyzer priced at €180, offering reliable, easy‑to‑use data for personal health monitoring, with optional subscription for analytics.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Employer Purchase Intent Test as outlined in the proposal.
final.uncertainty: Both demand for a consumer product and willingness to pay at €180 remain uncertain. Employer adoption is also uncertain due to lack of evidence.
would_change_if: If the test shows consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% and employer recommendation intent ≤ 10%, proceed with the consumer proposition.
If either condition fails, abandon consumer expansion and focus on existing B2B segments.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.

Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into a new B2B segment (e.g., commercial fishing or recreational boating) with a specialized distress-beacon solution.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they perceive a safety need and understand the technology's ability to transmit distress signals to search and rescue authorities.
T1.who_benefits: Recreational hikers, campers, and boaters in remote areas who currently rely on emergency radio or personal flares for distress signaling.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If these users learn that a 406 MHz beacon can automatically transmit a distress signal that can be detected by satellites and quickly relayed to SAR, they will be motivated to purchase it as a backup for existing signaling methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers or through outdoor recreation retailers, earning higher margins than B2B sales. Value is captured through premium pricing justified by the unique life‑saving capability.
assumptions: Consumers are aware of the FCC approval and the mandatory registration requirement for 406 MHz beacons.
There is sufficient trust in the technology to replace existing signaling methods.
Price sensitivity is moderate for a safety‑critical device.
predictions: If a survey of outdoor recreation groups shows >40% would purchase a 406 MHz beacon for emergency backup, the consumer proposition would be considered viable.
Sales in regions with high outdoor recreation density (e.g., national parks) would be higher than in low‑recreation density areas.
Willingness to pay would be above the €150 price point for basic models, reflecting the perceived safety benefit.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they perceive a safety need and understand the technology's ability to transmit distress signals to search and rescue authorities.

T2.claim: Emergency responders and search and rescue authorities will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons if they gain operational advantages such as faster detection, reduced false alarms, and improved situational awareness.
T2.who_benefits: SAR teams, coast guards, and other emergency services that currently rely on radio signals and visual observation for distress detection.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If these agencies learn that 406 MHz beacons can be automatically detected by satellites, reducing the time needed to pinpoint a distress signal, they will be motivated to acquire them for their operations.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons to government agencies and SAR contractors through B2B channels, earning higher margins than consumer sales. Value is captured through volume contracts and service contracts for beacon maintenance.
assumptions: SAR agencies are aware of the 406 MHz technology and its capabilities.
Budgetary constraints allow purchase of beacons for operational use.
There is a clear operational need that outweighs price concerns.
predictions: If a survey of SAR teams shows >30% would purchase 406 MHz beacons for operational purposes, the B2B proposition would be considered viable.
Sales in regions with high SAR activity (e.g., coastal states) would be higher than in low‑SAR density areas.
Willingness to pay would be above the €2,000 price point for professional models, reflecting the operational benefit.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If these users learn that a 406 MHz beacon can automatically transmit a distress signal that can be detected by satellites and quickly relayed to SAR, they will be motivated to purchase it as a backup for existing signaling methods.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers or through outdoor recreation retailers, earning higher margins than B2B sales. Value is captured through premium pricing justified by the unique life‑saving capability.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, technical feasibility, and potential value capture.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered from sources.
Alternatives include product redesign, new distribution channels, targeting a different customer group, or no expansion.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑focused distress‑beacon product for outdoor recreation (hiking, camping, boating) with a subscription service for emergency alerts.
2) Expand the existing marine survival light product line into consumer markets (e.g., outdoor enthusiasts, emergency preparedness kits) using the same technology.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on B2B/B2G markets (ships, aircraft, military, commercial marine) and existing consumer products without new consumer proposition.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they perceive them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals emergency services directly.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, boaters) gain peace of mind and emergency response capability.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of remote-area hazards and media coverage of survival stories create a perceived need for immediate distress communication.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge premium prices for a consumer-friendly device that integrates with existing emergency services, and can sell subscription services for alert monitoring.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in 2002 are sufficient to create a sizable market.
Consumers trust the technology to work in remote environments.
Regulatory requirements (e.g., mandatory registration) align with consumer expectations.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above standard survival lights.
Purchase intent will be higher when the device is presented as a safety-critical tool rather than a luxury item.
Subscription uptake will be driven by the perceived need for real-time alert monitoring.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a consumer-friendly device that can be integrated with local emergency dispatch systems, and can offer subscription services for alert monitoring and maintenance.
assumptions: Homeowners in 2002 have sufficient disposable income to purchase safety equipment.
Consumers trust the technology to work in home environments.
Regulatory requirements (e.g., mandatory registration) align with consumer expectations of safety compliance.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above standard survival lights.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed outdoor recreation vs SAR team messaging test to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent before committing resources. If the test confirms a 10% price premium and a 15-point purchase intent advantage for the outdoor description, proceed to develop a consumer product; otherwise, maintain the current B2B/B2G focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon if it is marketed as a safety-critical tool for remote travel, because they value emergency reliability and regulatory compliance.
T1.who_benefits: ACR Electronics gains sales and brand credibility in the outdoor market.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The 406 MHz frequency is mandated for emergency distress signals by the FCC and NOAA, and outdoor users already carry safety gear; adding a beacon aligns with existing safety protocols.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge a premium price for a certified, reliable device and sell through outdoor retailers and online channels.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to justify dedicated product development.
Consumers trust FCC/NOAA certification for safety.
Distribution channels exist for outdoor gear.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will express intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point above $300.
Sales of ACR’s existing 406 MHz EPIRB will increase if marketed as a safety-critical outdoor tool.
Competitor PLBs will be perceived as less reliable due to lack of regulatory mandate.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC and NOAA mandate the 406 MHz frequency for distress signaling, and SAR teams need reliable, interoperable devices to locate distressed individuals quickly.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell high-volume, standardized units to government and SAR agencies at contract prices, leveraging existing B2B relationships and compliance requirements.
assumptions: Government procurement budgets for SAR equipment exist in 2002.
SAR teams prioritize devices that meet regulatory standards over other features.
ACR’s existing EPIRBs meet the 406 MHz requirement.
predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz PLBs will increase in 2002.
Sales of ACR’s existing EPIRBs to SAR agencies will grow if marketed as compliant with regulatory mandates.
Competitors without a 406 MHz product will be excluded from government contracts.

X1.name: Outdoor Recreation vs SAR Team Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay questions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums and clubs) and (B) Emergency responders/SAR teams (recruited via professional associations and government procurement contacts). Each participant views a product description emphasizing either (A) safety-critical outdoor use (T1) or (B) emergency distress signaling for SAR teams (T2). They are then asked to state their maximum price they would pay for the device and their likelihood to purchase. The test
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 outdoor enthusiasts and 100 SAR/government procurement contacts. Recruitment via targeted online communities and professional networks.
X1.measure: Average maximum price willingness-to-pay (EUR) and purchase intent (percentage) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show higher willingness-to-pay and higher purchase intent when the product is described as a safety-critical outdoor tool compared to the SAR description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: SAR/government procurement contacts will show higher willingness-to-pay and higher purchase intent when the product is described as a mandated emergency distress beacon for SAR teams compared to the outdoor description.

X1.decision_rule: If the outdoor group's average willingness-to-pay for the outdoor description exceeds the SAR group's average willingness-to-pay for the SAR description by at least €50 (a 10% premium) and the purchase intent for the outdoor group is at least 15 percentage points higher, then T1 is

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer adoption, regulatory demand, or market size for 406 MHz distress beacons. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed outdoor recreation vs SAR team messaging test to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent before committing resources. If the test confirms a 10% price premium and a 15-point purchase intent advantage for the outdoor description, proceed to develop a consumer product; otherwise, maintain the current B2B/B2G focus.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, camping, boating) who value safety-critical gear and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress capability.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a safety-critical outdoor tool, emphasizing regulatory compliance, emergency reliability, and integration with existing outdoor gear.
final.next_action: Run the 8‑week, €15,000 messaging test with 200 participants (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 SAR/government procurement contacts). Measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent for outdoor vs SAR descriptions.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and market size for 406 MHz distress beacons in 2002.
would_change_if: If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts show no willingness to pay a premium or no purchase intent advantage, we would abandon the consumer proposition and continue B2B/B2G focus.
If the test shows SAR/government procurement contacts show a premium willingness to pay and higher intent, we would consider expanding to a SAR-focused product or licensing the technology.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
Must consider ACR’s existing B2B focus on ships, aircraft, and military/commercial marine users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote travel, and are willing to pay a premium for a reliable emergency device.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, climbers) who travel in remote areas where other distress methods are impractical.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners who need a practical, multipurpose lawn and garden tractor, leveraging the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers. Begin with a limited pilot of a basic model priced competitively, and use the results to decide whether to scale or pursue a premium branding strategy.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Investment decision must be based on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching the target market.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (status quo).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B dealer model for farm and industrial equipment.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a new subsidiary or spin‑out to create a consumer brand, leveraging Deere’s engineering but operating separately from the core business.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase them directly through existing dealer networks without a differentiated proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile, low‑cost gardening tool; Deere benefits by selling through its existing dealer network, capturing value through volume sales and dealer margins.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly growing small‑garden households need a machine that can mow, till, and pull small implements; a tractor that is easy to use and maintain offers a clear functional advantage over hand tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors at scale through its dealer network, earning per‑unit margins and building brand awareness among individual buyers.
assumptions: Small‑garden households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to purchase a lawn and garden tractor.
Deere’s dealer network can reach these households and provide adequate service.
The functional benefits of a tractor (versus hand tools) are understood and valued by target buyers.
predictions: If Deere introduces a basic lawn and garden tractor priced at a competitive level, dealers will report increased sales among individual buyers.
Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to purchase a tractor for multiple‑task use at a price point similar to existing competitive models.

assumptions: Suburban homeowners in 1962 have disposable income to afford premium consumer goods.

Deere can design and market a consumer‑focused tractor without compromising tractor performance.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two tractor concepts: a basic, functional model priced at a competitive level (e.g., $1,200) and a premium, aesthetically designed model priced at a higher level (e.g., $1,800). They are asked which they would purchase and how much they would pay. The survey also collects demographic data (age, household income, region).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25-65 who have small gardens (under 1/4 acre). Recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Percentage of participants choosing the basic model versus the premium model, and average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the basic model and WTP for the basic model will be within 10% of the competitive price point ($1,200).
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will choose the premium model and WTP for the premium model will be at least 20% above the competitive price point ($1,800).

X1.decision_rule: If the observed choice percentage for the premium model is at least 40% and its average WTP is at least $1,800, proceed with a premium consumer proposition. final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners who need a practical, multipurpose lawn and garden tractor, leveraging the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers. Begin with a limited pilot of a basic model priced competitively, and use the results to decide whether to scale or pursue a premium branding strategy.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with small gardens (under 1/4 acre) who need a versatile, low‑cost gardening tool.
final.value_proposition: A functional, competitively priced lawn and garden tractor that can mow, till, and pull small implements, sold through existing dealer networks, offering convenience and cost‑effectiveness.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (500 homeowners, 6 weeks, €15,000) to test whether a basic model wins at least 60% of choices and its average willingness‑to‑pay is within 10% of the competitive price point ($1,200).
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to functional demand and price sensitivity; there is no direct proof of premium branding demand or willingness to pay a premium. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows the premium model winning at least 40% of choices and its average WTP is at least $1,800, we would shift to a premium branding strategy.
If the basic model wins fewer than 60% of choices or its average WTP is outside the 10% range, we would reconsider expansion or license the technology to third parties.

Participants view a product description of a lawn tractor (specifications, price, and a brief description of its convenience/time‑saving benefits). They are then asked: "Which of the following best describes your primary reason for purchasing a lawn tractor?" (A) Convenience and time‑saving for yard work; (B) Status symbol and modern home‑owner signal; (C) Other (specify).

X1.measure: Percentage of participants selecting (A) as their primary reason. Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the tractor.

arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults aged 25‑65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region. Participants must have owned a lawn or garden tool in the past year.
arguments.measure: Percentage of participants selecting (A) as their primary reason. Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the tractor.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Homeowner Lawn and Garden Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are homeowners aged 25-65 in the United States who have a yard larger than 0.5 acre. They are shown a product description of a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor (Deere‑branded, 20 hp, 42‑inch deck) and asked: “What is the maximum price you would pay for this tractor?” They also indicate whether they would purchase it (yes/no).
X1.sample: 500 participants, recruited via an online panel to match the target demographic.
X1.measure: Average maximum price willing to pay (in euros) and purchase intent rate.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average maximum price will be at least 1.5 times the price of a comparable generic lawn mower (e.g., $500), and purchase intent will be at least 30% among participants who indicate they would purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average maximum price will be at least 1.2 times the price of a comparable generic lawn mower (e.g., $500), and purchase intent will be at least 40% among participants who indicate they would purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If average maximum price ≥ 1.5 * $500 ≥ €750 and purchase intent ≥ 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting convenience/time‑saving. If average maximum price ≥ 1.2 * $500 ≥ €600 and purchase intent ≥ 40%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting mechanization/durability. If neither threshold is met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address homeowner demand, willingness to pay, or the convenience/mechanization drivers of T1. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the survey meets the thresholds (average price ≥ €750, purchase intent ≥ 30%), proceed to develop a convenience/time-saving proposition; otherwise, maintain the status quo and focus on B2B dealer expansion.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with yards larger than 0.5 acre who need a mechanized solution for lawn and garden tasks.
final.value_proposition: A branded, consumer-grade lawn and garden tractor that reduces manual effort, integrates with existing tools, and is sold through existing dealer network, capturing higher margins through brand loyalty and recurring service contracts.
final.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget, targeting 500 homeowners aged 25‑65 in the United States.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a differentiated consumer proposition is uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of homeowner willingness to pay a premium for a single-tool solution. The survey is needed to test the thresholds.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness to pay ≥ €750 and purchase intent ≥ 30%, the recommendation would shift to develop the convenience/time-saving proposition.
If the survey shows average willingness to pay < €600 or purchase intent < 20%, the recommendation would remain to maintain the status quo and focus on B2B dealer expansion.
